Compose and publish the next work for my Missing Works music platform: a Bach-inspired sonata for violin and keyboard.

Please work through composition, revision, testing, and publication—not just a plan. Make routine musical and technical decisions yourself. Give me short progress updates and publish the finished piece when it is ready.

CONTEXT
The platform is live at https://lost-compositions.exe.xyz/
It hosts AI-composed homages, readable scores with sampled playback, composition notebooks, public conversation logs, and anonymous votes for future works.

The latest vote check found:
- Request ID: bach:violin-sonata:1
- Composer: Johann Sebastian Bach
- Form: violin-sonata
- Round: 1
- Votes: 1
- Status: open
No composition was started. Recheck live state before claiming the request; if another agent has already started or completed it, do not duplicate that work.

ACCESS AND SOURCE
- Local checkout: repo/
- Repository: https://github.com/akrentsel/beethovens-missing-quartet
- VM: ssh lost-compositions.exe.xyz
- [access detail removed]
- The entire website is hosted on the VM. GitHub is the source repository; old GitHub Pages links redirect to the VM.
- If the local checkout is unavailable, clone the repository.
- Check git status and current remote changes before editing. Preserve other people's uncommitted work.

READ FIRST
- README.md
- docs/composing.md
- deploy/README.md
- data/catalog.json
- deploy/public-files.txt
- Existing scores and the reusable player in work.html and assets/player.js.

Do not rebuild the platform. Add this work to the existing library.

CLAIM THE REQUEST
Read the queue:
ssh lost-compositions.exe.xyz 'sudo -u missingworks missing-works-admin queue --json'

If bach:violin-sonata:1 is still open, mark it in progress:
ssh lost-compositions.exe.xyz 'sudo -u missingworks missing-works-admin start bach:violin-sonata:1'

MUSICAL BRIEF
Write an original, complete sonata for violin and obbligato keyboard—not solo violin. Aim for four movements, slow–fast–slow–fast, roughly 10–15 minutes in total; musical coherence matters more than hitting a duration.

Bach's sonatas for violin and obbligato keyboard, BWV 1014–1019, are useful references for texture and form. Write new themes rather than lightly modifying an existing Bach tune. Document specific influences and any deliberate quotations honestly.

Make the keyboard a real contrapuntal partner, not just chords under a violin melody. Give the violin and keyboard upper voice meaningful dialogue, with a purposeful bass. Use imitation, sequences, suspensions, clear tonal destinations, and well-prepared cadences. Contrast the movements and give each a convincing ending.

Use piano playback to match the site's violin-sonata category. Choose the key and individual movement forms yourself. Include dynamics and articulation, but avoid imposing Beethoven's dramatic manner on Bach.

COMPOSITION AND CHECKS
- Store each movement as an ABC score under scores/, following existing conventions.
- Use the actual violin and keyboard parts, with appropriate clefs and MIDI programs. A violin staff plus keyboard treble and bass staves is a sensible starting point.
- Check durations, accidentals, ties, tuplets, instrument ranges, voice-leading, contrapuntal dissonance treatment, and cadences.
- Do a substantial musical revision pass after the first complete draft.
- Automated checks are evidence, not proof of good music. The earlier quartet checker in [local path removed] assumes four parts and uses a coarse timing grid; do not blindly apply it to this sonata.
- Sample playback has limitations: long bowed notes can run out after roughly six seconds, and fast strings can sound soft. Verify the actual rendered result.
- Do not say you listened if you only inspected notation or audio buffers.

PUBLIC COMPOSITION RECORD
As you work, give concise public updates explaining themes, formal choices, revisions, and test findings. Create:
1. A short composition notebook.
2. A searchable public transcript using the existing transcript interface as a model.

Use actual publishable messages, actions, and test results. Omit private internal reasoning, credentials, account details, and unrelated personal material; clearly mark omissions. Keep raw session exports outside the public repository and web directory.

PUBLISHING
Suggested work ID: bach-violin-sonata-1
Suggested title: Bach’s Missing Violin Sonata

Add a completed work manifest to data/catalog.json with:
- composerId: bach
- formId: violin-sonata
- round: 1
- The title, description, actual duration, ordered movements, score paths, and notebook/transcript links.

Preserve the existing Beethoven quartet and all voting data.

Update deploy/public-files.txt, run the relevant tests, and deploy an atomic public release to the VM according to deploy/README.md. Never deploy raw logs, credentials, server source, tests, or database files into the public website directory.

Test the deployed page in a browser: every movement renders and produces audio, controls work, navigation is correct, and the notebook/transcript links load. Commit and push the source changes.

Only after the work is publicly available and verified:
1. Copy the updated catalogue to /opt/missing-works/data/catalog.json on the VM.
2. Complete the request:
   ssh lost-compositions.exe.xyz 'sudo -u missingworks missing-works-admin complete bach:violin-sonata:1 bach-violin-sonata-1'

Completion preserves the votes and opens a new round. Do not reset the database or overwrite votes.

If you must abandon the composition, reopen the request rather than leave it permanently in progress.

Finish with the listening URL, a short guide to the movements, and an honest account of what was tested and what remains unverified.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Compile the .mw sources, copy the ABC into the repository's scores/ and publish a draft snapshot.
usage: pub.py "change note" [--dry-run]
The draft descriptor lists every movement whose source exists."""
import json, pathlib, subprocess, sys, re
ROOT = pathlib.Path('workspace/')
REPO = pathlib.Path('repo/')
MOVES = [('i', 'm1'), ('ii', 'm2'), ('iii', 'm3'), ('iv', 'm4')]
note = sys.argv[1]
dry = '--dry-run' in sys.argv
movements = []
for mid, stem in MOVES:
    src = ROOT / 'src' / f'{stem}.mw'
    if not src.exists():
        continue
    out = REPO / 'scores' / f'bach-violin-sonata-1-{mid}.abc'
    subprocess.run(['node', str(ROOT / 'tools/compile.js'), str(src), str(out)], check=True)
    text = out.read_text()
    label = re.search(r'^%%label (.*)$', text, re.M).group(1)
    mnote = re.search(r'^%%note (.*)$', text, re.M).group(1)
    movements.append({'id': mid, 'label': label, 'file': f'../missing-works/scores/{out.name}', 'note': mnote})
desc = {'id': 'bach-violin-sonata-1', 'requestId': 'bach:violin-sonata:1', 'title': 'Bach’s Missing Violin Sonata',
        'subtitle': 'Sonata in E minor for violin and keyboard',
        'description': 'An original AI-composed homage to Bach’s sonatas for violin and obbligato keyboard; work in progress.',
        'movements': movements}
(ROOT / 'draft.json').write_text(json.dumps(desc, ensure_ascii=False, indent=1))
revf = ROOT / 'draft.rev'
rev = int(revf.read_text()) if revf.exists() else 0
cmd = ['node', 'tools/publish-draft.mjs', '--manifest', str(ROOT / 'draft.json'), '--message', note, '--expect', str(rev)]
if dry:
    cmd.append('--dry-run')
r = subprocess.run(cmd, cwd=REPO, capture_output=True, text=True)
print(r.stdout[-1500:], r.stderr[-1500:])
if r.returncode == 0 and not dry:
    revf.write_text(str(rev + 1))
    with (ROOT / 'logs/drafts.log').open('a') as f:
        f.write(f'rev {rev + 1}: {note}\n')
sys.exit(r.returncode)

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Generate src/m3.mw: a canon at the octave, one bar apart, over a bass.
The follower is derived mechanically from the leader, so the canon is exact by construction."""
import re, pathlib
ROOT = pathlib.Path('workspace/')
NOTE = re.compile(r"([\^_]*)([A-Ga-g])([,']*)")

def shift(bar, octaves):
    """Move every note in a .mw bar by whole octaves. Decorations are kept as they are."""
    def one(m):
        acc, letter, marks = m.groups()
        o = (4 if letter.isupper() else 5) + marks.count("'") - marks.count(',') + octaves

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Choose the bass of the canon movement by dynamic programming.
The two canon voices are fixed. For every beat the search picks a chord from the local key that
fits the upper notes and a bass note (root or third preferred), and minimises: non-chord tones on
the beat, six-four chords, doubled leading notes, parallel fifths/octaves with either upper voice
(note-to-note and beat-to-beat) and awkward bass leaps. The result is a proposal, reviewed by hand."""
import json, subprocess, pathlib, itertools
ROOT = pathlib.Path('workspace/')

VN, RH = notes[0], notes[1]
BT, BARS = 48, 39
NB = BARS * 3
NAMES = ['C','^C','D','^D','E','F','^F','G','^G','A','^A','B']
def at(voice, t):

def scale(tonic, minor=False):
    steps = [0,2,3,5,7,8,10] if minor else [0,2,4,5,7,9,11]
    return [(tonic + x) % 12 for x in steps]
def chords(tonic, minor):

    lt = (tonic - 1) % 12; dom = (tonic + 7) % 12
    out.append(([dom, lt, (dom + 7) % 12], dom, True))                       # V (major)
    out.append(([dom, lt, (dom + 7) % 12, (dom + 10) % 12], dom, True))      # V7
    return out, lt
G, D, E, B = 7, 2, 4, 11
def region(bar):        # bar is 1-based
    if bar <= 4: return [(G, False)]
    if bar == 5: return [(G, False), (D, False)]
    if bar <= 16: return [(D, False)]
    if bar <= 21: return [(E, True)]
    if bar == 22: return [(E, True), (B, True)]
    if bar <= 26: return [(B, True)]
    return [(G, False)]
FIX = {}                                 # beat index -> forced bass pitch class
def fix(bar, beat, pc): FIX[(bar - 1) * 3 + beat - 1] = pc
fix(1,1,G); fix(8,3,9); fix(9,1,D); fix(16,3,9); fix(17,1,D); fix(17,2,D); fix(17,3,3); fix(18,1,E)
fix(26,3,6); fix(27,1,B); fix(27,2,B); fix(27,3,9); fix(28,1,G); fix(28,2,E); fix(28,3,0); fix(29,1,D); fix(29,2,D); fix(29,3,D)
fix(30,1,G); fix(37,3,D); fix(38,3,D); fix(39,1,G); fix(39,2,G); fix(39,3,G)
LOW, HIGH = 38, 55
def cands(b):
    bar = b // 3 + 1; t = b * BT
    on = [x for x in (at(VN, t), at(RH, t)) if x is not None]
    off = [x for x in (at(VN, t + 24), at(RH, t + 24)) if x is not None]
    res = {}
    for tonic, minor in region(bar):
        chs, lt = chords(tonic, minor)
        for tones, root, isdom in chs:
            fit = sum(0 if x % 12 in tones else 8 for x in on) + sum(0 if x % 12 in tones else 2 for x in off)
            for k, pc in enumerate(tones):
                inv = [0, 1.0, 5, 4][k]
                if pc == lt and any(x % 12 == lt for x in on + off): inv += 6
                if b in FIX and FIX[b] != pc: continue
                for p in range(LOW, HIGH + 1):
                    if p % 12 != pc: continue
                    if any(x < p + 3 for x in on + off): continue        # stay below the upper voices
                    # dissonance of the bass against the notes on the beat when they are chord tones is fine
                    c = fit + inv
                    if not on: c += 1
                    key = p
                    if key not in res or c < res[key][0]: res[key] = (c, tones)
    if b in FIX and not res:
        for p in range(LOW, HIGH + 1):
            if p % 12 == FIX[b]: res[p] = (0, [])
    return res
def last_before(voice, b):       # the note sounding just before beat b
    return at(voice, b * BT - 1)
def trans(b, p0, p1):
    c = 0; d = abs(p1 - p0)
    c += {0: 1.5, 1: 0, 2: 0, 3: 1, 4: 1, 5: 1, 7: 1, 12: 2.5}.get(d, 3.5 if d < 10 else 7)
    if d == 6: c += 3
    t = b * BT
    for voice in (VN, RH):
        y1 = at(voice, t)
        if y1 is None: continue
        for y0, w in ((last_before(voice, b), 60), (at(voice, t - BT), 20)):
            if y0 is None or y0 == y1 or p0 == p1: continue
            i0, i1 = (y0 - p0) % 12, (y1 - p1) % 12
            if i0 == i1 and i0 in (0, 7): c += w
            elif i1 in (0, 7) and (y1 - y0) * (p1 - p0) > 0 and abs(y1 - y0) > 2: c += 2   # direct fifth/octave by leap

for b in range(1, NB):

        if opts: best[b][p] = min(opts)
    if not best[b]: raise SystemExit(f'no candidate at beat {b} (bar {b // 3 + 1})')

for b in range(NB - 1, -1, -1):

line.reverse()
def tok(p):
    o = p // 12 - 1; name = NAMES[p % 12]
    return name + ',' * (4 - o)
bars = []

    else: bars.append(' '.join(tok(x) + 'z' for x in (a, bq, c)))
(ROOT / 'src/m3-bass.json').write_text(json.dumps(bars, indent=0))
for i in range(0, BARS, 6): print(i + 1, ' | '.join(bars[i:i + 6]))
EOF

The composition notebook

How Beethoven’s Missing Quartet was written, revised, and made playable.

An original AI-composed homage in D minor, not a rediscovered Beethoven work. Composed on November 14, 2026.

This is an edited, high-level account of the composition process, based on the recorded briefs, completion reports, score revisions, and test results. It is not a verbatim transcript or a disclosure of private internal reasoning. The musical judgments are analytical: the agents did not listen to the performance.

One small cell links four movements

The starting idea was to write a new quartet inspired by Beethoven’s middle-period language: concentrated motives, dialogue between instruments, abrupt changes of dynamics, and silences that interrupt an otherwise clear phrase.

A   B♭   C♯   D

A semitone up, a diminished seventh down, then a semitone up.

The minor-mode cell is transformed rather than quoted mechanically. Its major counterpart rises by step: A–B–C♯–D. That transformation connects the slow movement’s hymn, the scherzo’s trio, and the finale’s D-major coda.

One lead agent wrote movement I and built the player. Three subagents each wrote a different movement from a shared musical brief, then made a revision pass. The lead integrated the scores and checked their playback.

Each movement gives the cell a different role

I. Poco sostenuto. Allegro agitato

153 bars · approximately 6:22 · D minor · sonata form

The slow introduction introduces the cell from the cello upward through all four instruments. The Allegro turns it into a fortissimo octave motto, interrupted by quiet answers. A singing second theme moves to F major; the development darkens it and passes the cell through imitative entries.

The reprise briefly offers D major before the minor motto interrupts it. The coda remembers the slow introduction, then closes emphatically in D minor.

Revision and playback decisions

Flagged parallels were re-voiced in the accompaniment and cadences. The slow introduction’s tied notes were shortened by re-articulating them, because the sampled strings stop sustaining after about six seconds. Key changes needed a player fix to preserve the viola and cello clefs.

The composition notebook

How Bach’s Missing Violin Sonata was written, checked and revised.

An original AI-composed homage in E minor for violin and obbligato keyboard, not a rediscovered work by J. S. Bach. Composed on November 15, 2026, for the first request in the Missing Works voting queue.

This is an edited, high-level account based on the recorded messages, score revisions and test results. It is not a verbatim transcript or a disclosure of private internal reasoning. The musical judgments are analytical. The composing agent inspected notation and synthesised audio buffers; it did not listen to the music, and no person had reviewed it by ear when this page was written.

One motto, four movements

The sonata follows the slow–fast–slow–fast plan of Bach’s sonatas for violin and obbligato keyboard (BWV 1014–1019). The texture is theirs too: three real parts, with the violin and the keyboard’s right hand as equal partners over a bass that takes its share of the themes.

B   E   F♯   G

Up a fourth from the dominant, then two steps to the third of the key.

Every movement begins from this rising figure. The Adagio holds its last note as a suspension. The fugue turns it into running quavers. The canon states it in G major (D–G–A–B) and, in its middle, brings back the E minor form in the keyboard. The gigue sets it in dotted dance rhythm and then turns it upside down.

What is borrowed, and what is not

  • No quotations. The themes were written for this piece. The motto itself is a common Baroque opening shape, not a tune taken from Bach.
  • A stock formula in the fugue subject. After the motto, the subject leaps up to the sixth degree and drops a diminished seventh to the leading note (G, E, C, D♯, E). That falling diminished seventh is a formula shared by many Baroque minor-key subjects, including Handel’s “And with His stripes” and the A minor fugue in Book II of the Well-Tempered Clavier. It is used here deliberately as a formula; the notes around it are new.
  • The canon’s model. The third movement of Bach’s A major sonata, BWV 1015, is a canon between violin and right hand over a detached bass. Movement III takes that idea. Its notes, metre (3/4), key and canon interval (the octave) are its own.
  • General habits of the style. A lament bass that sinks by semitones, chains of suspensions round the circle of fifths, a da capo design for the fugal Allegro, and a gigue whose second half inverts the subject are all common Baroque procedures.

The movements

I. Adagio

20 bars · approximately 2:06 · E minor

The violin states a two-bar subject over a bass that descends E–D–C–B. The right hand plays a counter-melody, then the two upper parts exchange roles and the music turns to G major. A chain of sevenths leads to B minor, where the bass takes the subject. A second chain returns towards E minor. Then the bass sinks by semitones from E to B while the violin climbs against it. The subject returns in the right hand under a violin descant, an interrupted cadence and a Neapolitan sixth delay the close, and the motto is heard once more over a tonic pedal before a major ending.

Read the ABC score

II. Allegro

51 bars · approximately 2:33 · E minor · fugue in da capo form

The violin gives the subject with a bass accompaniment; the right hand answers in B minor while the violin adds a countersubject in short-short-long figures; the bass enters third. An episode passes the subject’s first notes between the upper parts over a running bass. A stretto follows (right hand, violin in its lowest register, bass), then the subject’s head over a dominant pedal and a close. The middle section brings entries in G major, D major, A minor (bass) and B minor, separated by episodes, and cadences in B minor. The opening section then returns complete.

Read the ABC score

III. Andante un poco

40 written bars · approximately 3:07 with the repeat · G major · canon at the octave

The violin leads and the right hand follows one bar later, an octave lower, over a detached bass; the first half moves to D major and is repeated. In the middle the roles are reversed: the right hand leads in E minor with the sonata’s opening motto and the violin follows an octave higher, ending in B minor. A short free passage leads back, and the canon closes in G. The follower is generated from the leader by a program, so the canon is exact wherever the score says it is.

Read the ABC score

IV. Allegro

39 bars in two repeated halves · approximately 1:52 · E minor · fugal gigue

The motto becomes a gigue subject. Violin, right hand (in B minor) and bass enter in turn, a chain of sevenths follows, and the first half closes in B minor. After the double bar the subject returns upside down, again in all three parts. A cadence in G major and a turn to the dominant lead to the subject and its inversion sounding together, a last bass entry, and a close over a dominant pedal.

Read the ABC score

How it was checked

  • Sounding-pitch sources. Each movement was written in a small source format in which every note carries its sounding accidental. A compiler writes the ABC and the accidentals that standard notation needs, so a forgotten key signature or bar accidental cannot change a pitch.
  • A three-part counterpoint checker written for this piece reads the notes exactly as the player’s library will play them. It reports bar lengths, ranges, long violin notes, parallel and beat-to-beat fifths and octaves between every pair of parts, cross relations, augmented melodic steps, and each dissonance with how it is approached and left. The earlier quartet checker was not used: it assumes four parts and a coarse time grid.
  • The canon’s bass was first written by hand and kept producing parallel octaves with the two canon voices. It was replaced by a search that picks, beat by beat, a chord and bass note that fit both voices at the lowest voice-leading cost. The result was then reviewed and partly fixed by hand where the search chose a weak progression.
  • Rendering in the real player. Every movement was rendered in the site’s player in headless Chrome, and the audio buffers were measured with all parts and with each part alone.

What the checks found, and what changed

  • First drafts contained many parallel octaves and fifths, mostly between the bass and a part it doubled. They were removed by changing bass figures, inverting chords or altering a decoration. Several subject and countersubject details changed for the same reason; for example the Adagio subject now holds its G through the fourth beat instead of resolving on it.
  • Balance. In the rendered buffers the violin sample was about four times (roughly 12 dB) stronger than either keyboard hand at the same written dynamic in this texture, which would have buried the right hand. The scores therefore mark the violin several levels below the keyboard (violin ppp–p, keyboard mf–ff).
